source.title: Decode-gLM: Tools to Interpret, Audit, and Steer Genomic Language Models
source.authors: Aaron Maiwald; Piotr Jedryszek; Florent Draye; B. Schölkopf; Garrett M. Morris; O. Crook

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses the premise that neurons can be polysemantic to motivate sparse autoencoders, then applies SAEs to discover genomic features. It does not measure the claim versions’ neuron-pole shares or evaluate their other specified claims.
record.gate_note: The paper does compare interpretable SAE latents with MLP latents, but this is not an audit of the one-job/two-job/unknown shares in the claim versions. The text gives only qualitative comparisons for these results; Figure 2a contains the underlying plotted values.
record.test_reason: The paper takes polysemanticity and superposition as its premise and trains SAEs on Nucleotide Transformer MLP outputs to find biological features. Its only neuron-level result compares counts and F1-scores of MLP-output dimensions against SAE latents, using plasmid annotations and an F1 ≥ 20% cut-off. It does not audit neuron poles into one-job, two-job or unexplained shares. It does not test InceptionV1 neurons, attribution graphs, or explanation-simulation scoring. The MLP-versus-SAE comparison is the study's own method against a baseline, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state as their central hypothesis that genomic LM activations encode biological properties in superposition, which SAEs disentangle. They conclude SAEs suit feature discovery, dataset auditing (CMV contamination) and steering (A1408G), and that meta-SAEs reveal hierarchical concepts.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on genomic-model MLP activations and evaluates their association with biological annotations; it does not use the neuron-pole auditing procedure described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The number of interpretable SAE latents varied strongly across layers; the largest model was evaluated only at layer 10.

fits_no_version.finding: In the 50m Nucleotide Transformer, across layers 1, 4, 7, 10 and 12, SAE latents with F1 ≥ 20% for a plasmid annotation far outnumbered MLP-output dimensions meeting the same cut-off. The top SAE latents also had consistently higher F1 (Fig. 2a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a genomic masked language model, SAE latents align with annotated biological concepts more often and more strongly than raw MLP-output dimensions, under an F1-against-annotation criterion.

record.code_released: COMING SOON (the paper provides no code URL)
record.problems: The neuron-relevant comparisons are reported qualitatively in the text, with exact counts and F1-scores available only in a figure; they do not measure the claim’s pole categories or shares.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares: ~90% one job, ~7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood.
Similar pole shares in other language models, dense and MoE, up to trillions of parameters. The genomic model's MLP-output dimensions are not audited into these categories.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons (InceptionV1 cat/car) as recursive generalization.
Whether the share of interpretable neurons rises with better tools and architectures, and the causes of messy late-layer neurons.
Attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons, without a replacement model.
Whether explanations drawn from activating examples predict where neurons fire.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The 'MLP latents' here are dimensions of the MLP output, not MLP hidden neurons, so even read loosely this is not a neuron-pole audit. Interpretability is defined by the F1 cut-off against a fixed annotation set (pLannotate), which would undercount neurons with jobs outside that set. Neuron results are figure-only. The study is a preprint and code is not yet released.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares and the stated one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood categories.
Shares of neuron poles across other language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons and recursive generalization versus superposition.
The proposed causes of messy late-layer neurons and the claimed change in interpretable-neuron share with tools or architecture.
Attribution graphs made from a large model’s own neurons and their reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: 50m Nucleotide Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared counts of interpretable MLP latents and SAE latents, defining interpretability as F1-score of at least 20% for an annotation.
rows.baseline: SAE-latent count; stated to be higher than the MLP-latent count across layers
rows.value: The number of interpretable MLP latents was lower than the number of interpretable SAE latents across layers; exact values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The paper reports this as an aggregate qualitative comparison across the listed layers; numerical counts are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: This is the study's method (SAE) compared with a baseline. The units are MLP output dimensions rather than MLP hidden neurons or their poles. The 'interpretable' cut-off is F1 ≥ 20% against plasmid annotations, not a one-main-job judgment, so it cannot show V1/V2 shares. Exact counts appear only in Fig. 2a. The baseline field is inverted: the MLP count is the baseline and the SAE count is the value.

source_check.notes: Both rows are method-vs-baseline comparisons (SAE latents vs MLP output dimensions, not hidden neurons; Domain F1 at least 20% on pLannotate plasmid annotations).
